cards.question: Is a photo a record of what was there?
cards.answer: Partly a reconstruction. Each pixel on a camera sensor measures only one colour, behind a red, green or blue filter. The other two values are interpolated from the neighbours. Every ordinary digital photograph is roughly two-thirds informed guesswork, done well enough that nobody notices.
cards.move: Two of every three colour values in your photos were guessed.
cards.source: Bayer filter demosaicing, standard in digital sensors
cards.reference: Bayer, Color imaging array, US Patent 3,971,065, 1976

cards.question: Why are blockbusters orange and teal?
cards.answer: Skin tones sit in the orange range, and teal is directly opposite on the colour wheel — so pushing shadows teal makes faces jump forward. Digital grading made the move cheap and instant in the 2000s, and a look that once took effort became the default.
cards.move: Faces are orange, so the shadows went teal. That is the whole reason.
cards.reference: Misek, Chromatic Cinema: A History of Screen Color, Wiley-Blackwell, 2010

cards.question: What does GDP actually count?
cards.answer: Activity, not wellbeing. A car crash raises it: the ambulance, the repairs, the legal fees all count. Cleaning up after a hurricane counts. Raising your own children does not. Simon Kuznets, who built the measure in 1934, warned in the same report that it should never be read as welfare.
cards.move: GDP counts the crash and ignores the childcare. That was known from day one.

cards.question: How do the world's flowers get priced?
cards.answer: Mostly through a few enormous clocks in the Netherlands. At the Aalsmeer auction the price starts high and counts down until a buyer stops it — so hesitating costs you the lot. A large share of the cut flowers sold worldwide passes through that building within hours of being cut.
cards.move: Most of the world's flowers are priced by a clock running backwards.
cards.reference: Royal FloraHolland, Annual Report, 2022

cards.question: What made global manufacturing possible?
cards.answer: A steel box. Before standard containers, cargo was loaded piece by piece and moving goods across an ocean could cost a substantial fraction of their value. Standardising the box — not the ship — collapsed that cost until where something is made stopped depending much on where it is sold.
cards.move: The container, not the ship, is what moved the factories.

cards.question: Can average pay rise while everyone earns less?
cards.answer: Yes. If well-paid jobs grow as a share of the workforce, the average can climb even when pay falls within every single group. The overall number and the group-by-group numbers can point in opposite directions, and both are correct — which is why the headline needs the breakdown.
cards.move: An average can rise while every part of it falls.
cards.reference: Wagner, Simpson's Paradox in Real Life, The American Statistician, 1982

cards.question: How much can an insurance loss cost one person?
cards.answer: Everything they own. Until the 1990s, the individuals backing Lloyd's of London — the "Names" — carried unlimited personal liability. Asbestos claims written decades earlier surfaced at once and ruined thousands of them, over policies most had never read for risks nobody had priced.
cards.move: They had unlimited liability. The word unlimited was meant literally.
cards.source: Lloyd's of London, asbestos and the Names, 1988-1996
cards.reference: Duguid, On the Brink: How a Crisis Transformed Lloyd's of London, Palgrave Macmillan, 2014

cards.question: Should cities scrap rules requiring new buildings to include parking spaces?
cards.answer: A mandated parking space adds serious cost to every flat built, whether or not the resident owns a car — so renters without cars subsidise those with them. The requirement also forces buildings apart, which is what makes a district need a car in the first place.
cards.move: Both sides agree the cost is real. They disagree about who is currently paying it.
cards.counterpoint: Remove the minimum and the cars do not vanish; they park on streets that were not built for them, and the cost lands on everyone who lives there rather than on the developer. In places with weak public transport, a building with no parking is a building only car-free households can use.
cards.reference: Shoup, The High Cost of Free Parking, Planners Press, 2005

cards.question: Should people be allowed to bet real money on election results?
cards.answer: A market makes people pay for being wrong, which is why prediction markets have often beaten polls. Money in the market is information nobody else is collecting, and banning it does not stop forecasting — it just leaves it to pundits who face no cost for a bad call.
cards.move: The forecasting argument and the manipulation argument are both correct, which is what makes this hard.
cards.counterpoint: A market on an outcome that people can influence is a market with an incentive to influence it. Enough money on a result gives someone a reason to suppress turnout, seed a story, or worse, and the sums that would move a contract are small next to the sums already in politics.
cards.reference: Wolfers & Zitzewitz, Prediction Markets, Journal of Economic Perspectives, 2004

cards.question: Should anyone be able to sit a degree's final exams without attending the university?
cards.answer: If the exam certifies the knowledge, then the knowledge is what should be certified, however it was acquired. Locking the assessment behind three years of fees turns a measure of competence into a measure of who could afford to be measured.
cards.move: What is on the exam and what the degree is for may be two different things.
cards.counterpoint: Most of what a degree gives is not on the exam: the supervision, the arguing, the lab where you learn what an experiment feels like when it fails. Certify only the testable part and universities will drift towards teaching only the testable part.
cards.reference: Kenyon Jones, The People's University: 150 Years of the University of London and its External Students, University of London, 2008

cards.question: Why did container ships get slower?
cards.answer: Deliberately, after 2008. Fuel use rises steeply with speed, so cutting speed by around a tenth saves a disproportionate share of the fuel. When freight rates collapsed and fuel stayed dear, slowing down beat sailing fast — and much of the fleet never sped back up.
cards.move: The world's cargo slowed down on purpose and mostly stayed slow.
cards.source: Slow steaming, adopted across container shipping post-2008
cards.reference: Cariou, Is slow steaming a sustainable means of reducing CO2 emissions from container shipping?, Transportation Research Part D, 2011

cards.question: Is there a human fingerprint on the ice cores before industry?
cards.answer: There is a dip. Atmospheric CO2 fell in the early 1600s, and the timing matches the collapse of the Americas' population after 1492. Tens of millions of hectares of farmland reverted to forest, and the regrowth pulled down enough carbon to show up in ice.
cards.move: A population collapse is visible in the ice, two centuries before the factories.
cards.source: Koch et al., Quaternary Science Reviews, 2019
cards.reference: Koch, Brierley, Maslin & Lewis, Earth system impacts of the European arrival and Great Dying in the Americas after 1492, Quaternary Science Reviews, 2019

cards.question: How do you date something from the last seventy years?
cards.answer: By the bomb. Atmospheric nuclear testing from 1955 to 1963 nearly doubled carbon-14 in the air, then it declined on a known curve. Anything alive during that window carries a datable signature, accurate to a year or two — used on forged paintings, wine and human remains.
cards.move: Nuclear testing accidentally left the world a precise clock.
cards.reference: Levin & Kromer, The tropospheric 14CO2 level in mid-latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere (1959-2003), Radiocarbon, 2004

cards.question: What killed soldiers in the nineteenth century?
cards.answer: Disease, not the enemy — by a wide margin in most campaigns. Florence Nightingale's real achievement was statistical: she invented diagrams that made the ratio impossible to argue with, because the officials who could change things would not read a table.
cards.move: She is remembered for the lamp. The argument was won with a chart.
cards.source: Nightingale, Notes on Matters Affecting the Health of the British Army, 1858

cards.question: When was aluminium a luxury metal?
cards.answer: In the 1850s. It is one of the commonest elements in the crust but was brutally hard to separate, so it cost more than gold — Napoleon III is said to have reserved aluminium cutlery for his most important guests. A new electrolytic process collapsed the price within about a decade.
cards.move: Aluminium went from imperial cutlery to disposable foil in one lifetime.

cards.question: Where did modern finance and science actually meet?
cards.answer: In coffee houses. Seventeenth-century London called them "penny universities": the price of entry bought conversation. Lloyd's insurance market began in one, newspapers grew out of them, and scientific societies used them as informal meeting rooms before they had buildings.
cards.move: Lloyd's of London started as a coffee shop with good shipping gossip.
cards.source: Ellis, The Coffee House: A Cultural History, 2004

cards.question: How big is your blind spot?
cards.answer: Each eye has a hole in its field of view where the optic nerve leaves — large enough to swallow several full moons at arm's length. You never see it, because the brain fills the gap with a guess based on the surrounding pattern. The guess is usually right, which is the unsettling part.
cards.move: Your brain is painting over a hole in your vision. Continuously.
cards.source: Ramachandran, Nature, filling-in of the blind spot

cards.question: How old is your skeleton?
cards.answer: Younger than you. Bone is torn down and rebuilt continuously by two kinds of cell, and the adult skeleton turns over roughly every ten years. The shape persists; the material does not. What you feel as the most permanent part of the body is among the most rebuilt.
cards.move: Your skeleton is about ten years old, whatever your birthday says.

cards.question: Does your gut have a brain?
cards.answer: It has a nervous system of its own — hundreds of millions of neurons in the wall of the intestine — and it keeps coordinating digestion when the connection to the brain is severed. It is the only organ system that can run its reflexes without asking.
cards.move: The gut keeps working with the line to head office cut.

cards.question: Why does that shirt match indoors and clash outside?
cards.answer: Because colour vision takes only three samples of a continuous spectrum. Two objects reflecting quite different light can produce identical signals — a metameric match — under one light and separate under another. The colours did not change. The sampling did.
cards.move: Two colours can be the same colour, until you carry them to a window.
cards.reference: Wyszecki & Stiles, Color Science: Concepts and Methods, Quantitative Data and Formulae, Wiley, 1982

cards.question: What makes a heart beat?
cards.answer: The heart does. A cluster of pacemaker cells generates its own rhythm, and the brain only speeds it up or slows it down. A heart removed from the body and supplied with oxygen keeps beating on its own — which is precisely why transplantation is possible.
cards.move: The brain does not start the heartbeat. It only argues about the tempo.

cards.question: Is there a word every language shares?
cards.answer: Possibly one. "Huh?" — the sound for signalling you did not catch something — appears in essentially every language studied, with a strikingly similar form. It looks less like a word inherited from a common ancestor and more like one every language independently converges on, because conversation needs it.
cards.move: Every language on record has its own version of "huh?", and they all sound alike.
cards.reference: doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0078273

cards.question: What was writing invented for?
cards.answer: Accounting. The oldest substantial writing is Mesopotamian bookkeeping: receipts for grain, beer and livestock, and records of who owed what. Literature comes many centuries later. Writing began as an administrative technology and was only afterwards turned to anything anyone would read for pleasure.
cards.move: The first thing anyone wrote down was a receipt.

cards.question: How many colours does a language need?
cards.answer: No — and the ones that gain colour terms do so in a remarkably consistent order. Dark and light come first, then red, then green or yellow, and blue late. Languages carve the same continuous spectrum into different numbers of words, in more or less the same sequence.
cards.move: Blue is one of the last colours a language gets a word for.

cards.question: Are sign languages signed versions of speech?
cards.answer: Not at all — they have their own grammar, unrelated to the surrounding spoken language. The clearest proof arrived in 1980s Nicaragua, where deaf children brought together for the first time built a full language from scratch within a couple of school generations.
cards.move: Deaf children in Nicaragua invented a complete language in about a decade.
cards.reference: Senghas & Coppola, Children creating language: How Nicaraguan Sign Language acquired a spatial grammar, Psychological Science, 2001

cards.question: Why was silent reading once remarkable?
cards.answer: Because text was written to be spoken. Early manuscripts ran words together with little punctuation, and reading aloud was how you parsed them. Augustine noted with some surprise that Ambrose read without moving his lips. Spacing and punctuation are technologies for reading quietly.
cards.move: The space between words is an invention, and a fairly late one.
cards.reference: Saenger, Space Between Words: The Origins of Silent Reading, Stanford University Press, 1997

cards.question: Did we create antibiotic resistance?
cards.answer: We selected it; we did not invent it. Genes conferring resistance to several antibiotic classes have been recovered from 30,000-year-old permafrost, long before any human made a drug. Resistance is an ancient feature of microbial life that our use of antibiotics turned into an emergency.
cards.move: Resistance genes are older than agriculture.
cards.reference: D'Costa et al., Antibiotic resistance is ancient, Nature, 2011

cards.question: Should organ donation be opt-out by default, so everyone is a donor unless they register otherwise?
cards.answer: Defaults decide outcomes for anything people do not get round to. Most people say they support donation and never register, so opt-in measures paperwork rather than willingness. Countries that switched report more organs available, and objecting stays a single form away.
cards.move: The default changed the register. Whether it changed the operating theatre is a separate question.
cards.counterpoint: The jump in donations in opt-out countries mostly tracks transplant infrastructure and how families are approached, not the default itself — Spain's results came years after its law. And consent that was never given is not consent: families asked at the worst hour of their lives may refuse harder when the state has already assumed an answer.
cards.reference: Arshad, Anderson & Sharif, Comparison of organ donation and transplantation rates between opt-out and opt-in systems, Kidney International, 2019

cards.question: Should volunteers be deliberately infected with a disease to test a vaccine faster?
cards.answer: A challenge trial can answer in weeks what a field trial answers in a year, and during an epidemic that gap is counted in deaths. Healthy adult volunteers already accept comparable risks in kidney donation and firefighting, and the risk here is bounded, monitored and reversible.
cards.move: Notice the argument is not about the numbers. It is about who is allowed to accept a risk on behalf of everyone.
cards.counterpoint: You cannot fully consent to a disease nobody has yet characterised, and the volunteers most willing to sign up are often those with the least to fall back on. A single death in a trial where the researchers caused the infection would be a very different event, both morally and for every trial that came after it.
cards.reference: Eyal, Lipsitch & Smith, Human Challenge Studies to Accelerate Coronavirus Vaccine Licensure, Journal of Infectious Diseases, 2020

cards.question: Should we screen healthy people for cancer earlier and more often?
cards.answer: Screening moves a diagnosis from late to early, and early is where treatment works. Someone whose tumour is caught at stage one gets a different life from someone caught at stage three, and the cost of a scan is trivial against the cost of chemotherapy.
cards.move: Survival going up and deaths going down are not the same measurement, and only one of them is the point.
cards.counterpoint: In a population where the disease is rare, most positives are false, and each one buys biopsies, anxiety and sometimes surgery. Screening also finds tumours that would never have caused harm, and treating those is pure loss. Five-year survival rises whenever you diagnose earlier, even when the date of death does not move at all.
cards.reference: Welch & Black, Overdiagnosis in Cancer, Journal of the National Cancer Institute, 2010

cards.question: Should drug patents be shorter than twenty years?
cards.answer: The monopoly is paid for in lives: people who cannot afford a drug that costs cents to manufacture. A shorter term still rewards invention while moving the moment of cheap generics closer, and much of the underlying science was publicly funded anyway.
cards.move: Both sides are arguing about the same number from different ends of the development timeline.
cards.counterpoint: The patent clock starts at discovery, not at approval, so a drug that spends a decade in trials may see only a few protected years already. Cut it further and the projects that die first are the slow ones — antibiotics, rare diseases — where the payback was marginal to begin with.
cards.reference: Kesselheim, Avorn & Sarpatwari, The High Cost of Prescription Drugs in the United States: Origins and Prospects for Reform, JAMA, 2016

cards.question: When a treatment that works already exists, should new drugs still be tested against a sugar pill?
sides: No, test against the best existing drug
cards.answer: A placebo arm is the cleanest measurement there is, needs fewer patients, and answers the question that regulators actually ask. Against an existing drug you can only show something is not much worse, which is how a slow drift towards weaker medicines begins.
cards.move: The cleanest experiment and the useful question are pulling in opposite directions here.
cards.counterpoint: It means deliberately giving a patient nothing when something known to help exists. And the answer it produces is not the one anybody needs: no doctor is choosing between this drug and nothing, they are choosing between this drug and the one already on the shelf.
cards.reference: World Medical Association, Declaration of Helsinki, 2013 revision

cards.question: What fertilises the Amazon?
cards.answer: Dust from Chad. Heavy rain strips phosphorus out of rainforest soil, and the shortfall is largely made up by dust blown across the Atlantic from the Bodele Depression — a dried lakebed that supplies a striking share of the phosphorus reaching the basin each year.
cards.move: The Amazon is fed by a dried-up lake three thousand miles away.
cards.source: Yu et al., Geophysical Research Letters, 2015

cards.question: Why is the world running out of sand?
cards.answer: Because desert sand is useless for building. Wind rounds the grains smooth so they will not lock together in concrete; construction needs angular river and seabed sand. Demand has outrun supply enough to support organised theft and illegal dredging.
cards.move: A country can sit in a desert and still have to import sand.
cards.reference: UNEP, Sand and Sustainability: Finding new solutions for environmental governance of global sand resources, 2019

cards.question: How would you know if the ocean used to be fuller?
cards.answer: You probably would not. Each generation of scientists takes the sea they first studied as the natural baseline, so every generation measures decline from an already-depleted state. Daniel Pauly named this shifting baseline syndrome, and it makes long collapses look like normal variation.
cards.move: Everyone measures the decline from whatever they found when they arrived.
cards.reference: Pauly, Anecdotes and the shifting baseline syndrome of fisheries, Trends in Ecology & Evolution, 1995

cards.question: What was the largest mass extinction caused by?
cards.answer: Life inventing photosynthesis. Cyanobacteria began releasing oxygen roughly 2.4 billion years ago — lethal to almost everything then alive, and it stripped out the methane keeping the planet warm. The organisms that made the air we need caused one of the worst catastrophes in the record.
cards.move: The first great extinction was pollution, produced by life itself.

cards.question: Do trees really share food through a fungal network?
cards.answer: Less than the story suggests. Trees are certainly connected to fungi, but the claim that they deliberately send resources to their neighbours rests on a small number of studies, several of which do not support it on re-reading. Recent reviews find the popular version outran the evidence.
cards.move: The wood wide web is real. The generosity is not established.
cards.source: Karst, Jones & Hoeksema, Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2023
cards.reference: Karst, Jones & Hoeksema, Positive citation bias and overinterpreted results lead to misinformation on common mycorrhizal networks in forests, Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2023

cards.question: True or false: the Amazon supplies about a fifth of the oxygen people breathe?
cards.answer: False. The forest makes plenty of oxygen and uses almost all of it again: trees respire about half, and microbes rotting its leaves and wood take most of the rest. Its net contribution is close to zero. The oxygen in the air is a stock laid down over hundreds of millions of years.
cards.move: Before crediting a producer, subtract what it uses up itself.
cards.trap: Counting the oxygen a forest makes and forgetting what it burns.
cards.reference: https://nature.ox.ac.uk/research_stories/rainforests-are-not-the-lungs-of-our-planet/

cards.question: Did cleaning up shipping fuel warm the planet?
cards.answer: Yes, measurably. Ships burned high-sulphur fuel that seeded brighter clouds over the oceans, reflecting sunlight. A 2020 rule cut that sulphur by around 80% almost overnight, the clouds dimmed, and one climate model puts the extra warming at up to three years' worth.
cards.move: One pollution rule ran the planet's most accidental experiment.

cards.question: Two drunk drivers, one hits a child. Are they equally guilty?
cards.answer: Both made the same decision and took the same risk; only one had a child step out. We punish them very differently, and most people feel that is right. But the difference was luck, and if luck can change how blameworthy you are, control is not what blame rests on.
cards.move: The only difference between the two drivers was who walked into the road.
cards.reference: Williams & Nagel, Moral Luck, Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society, Supplementary Volume 50, 1976

cards.question: Two boxes. Do you take one or both?
cards.answer: A reliable predictor has already put a million in box B if it foresaw you taking B alone, and nothing if it foresaw you taking both. Box A holds a thousand either way. Taking both dominates. Taking B alone has a far better track record. Decision theorists still split on it.
cards.move: Two solid arguments, opposite answers, fifty years and no resolution.
cards.source: Nozick, Newcomb's Problem and Two Principles of Choice, 1969
cards.reference: Nozick, Newcomb's Problem and Two Principles of Choice, in Essays in Honor of Carl G. Hempel, Reidel, 1969

cards.question: When does a heap stop being a heap?
cards.answer: Remove one grain from a heap and it is still a heap. Repeat. Somewhere it stops, but no single grain did it. This is not wordplay: the same structure decides who counts as poor enough for support, or ill enough for treatment. A line gets drawn where nature has none.
cards.move: Every threshold in every policy is one grain of sand away from arbitrary.
cards.source: The sorites paradox, attributed to Eubulides
cards.reference: Williamson, Vagueness, Routledge, 1994

cards.question: Is survival what you actually care about?
cards.answer: Parfit argued not. If you were replaced by someone psychologically continuous with you, what matters to you would carry on — so the question "but would it be me?" may be empty rather than hard. He wrote that seeing this made his own death seem less bad.
cards.move: Parfit's claim: identity is not what matters. Continuity is.
cards.reference: Parfit, Reasons and Persons, Oxford University Press, 1984, p. 281

cards.question: Is a bigger world a better one?
cards.answer: Take a happy population. Adding people whose lives are worth living seems no worse. Repeat, trading a little quality for more numbers each time, and you arrive at an enormous population whose lives are barely worth living — rated better than the first. Forty years on, nobody has an agreed way out.
cards.move: Every reasonable-looking rule about population leads somewhere nobody accepts.
cards.source: Parfit, Reasons and Persons, 1984; the repugnant conclusion
cards.reference: Parfit, Reasons and Persons, Oxford University Press, 1984, part four

cards.question: Should peer review be signed rather than anonymous?
cards.answer: Anonymity protects the reviewer who kills a rival's paper, sits on it for eight months, or demands their own work be cited. A name attached to a judgement makes the judgement more careful, and readers can finally see who vouched for what.
cards.move: Whichever you picked, the question is who carries the cost of an honest opinion.
cards.counterpoint: The junior reviewer who signs a hard review of a powerful lab is the one who pays for it, at their next grant or job application. Remove anonymity and criticism does not become fairer, it becomes quieter — and the people it goes quiet for are exactly those with the most power already.
cards.reference: Ross-Hellauer, What is open peer review? A systematic review, F1000Research, 2017

cards.question: What is the most reused six seconds in music?
cards.answer: A drum break from The Winstons' 1969 B-side "Amen, Brother". Sampled into hip-hop, then sped up into jungle and drum and bass, it underpins thousands of records across decades. The drummer, Gregory Coleman, received nothing for it and died without a home.
cards.move: Six seconds of drums from 1969 built two entire genres.
cards.reference: The Winstons, Color Him Father / Amen, Brother, Metromedia Records, 1969

cards.question: Why did records get louder for thirty years?
cards.answer: Because louder sounds better in a first comparison, so each release pushed the level up — flattening the quiet parts until the dynamics were gone. Streaming ended the incentive by normalising loudness on playback, so a squashed master now just sounds squashed.
cards.move: The loudness war ended when the platforms turned everything down equally.
cards.reference: Vickers, The Loudness War: Background, Speculation and Recommendations, Audio Engineering Society Convention Paper 8175, 2010

cards.question: Whose laughter is on old sitcoms?
cards.answer: Often people who died decades before the show aired. Most canned laughter came from a single machine, the Laff Box, built and jealously guarded by one engineer who recorded audiences in the 1950s. The same chuckles recur across hundreds of programmes.
cards.move: That laugh track is a recording of an audience from the 1950s.
cards.source: Charles Douglass and the Laff Box

cards.question: How were television ratings actually measured?
cards.answer: By a few thousand households standing in for a nation. Nielsen fitted meters to a small sample and extrapolated; shows lived or died on the result. Whole genres disappeared because the sample did not happen to contain many of the people who watched them.
cards.move: A few thousand homes decided what a hundred million people could watch.

cards.question: Why do IQ tests keep being rescored?
cards.answer: Because raw scores kept rising — roughly three points a decade through the 20th century, across many countries. Tests are re-normed to keep the average at 100, which hides the drift. Score as an average adult today and you would have sat near the top of the distribution a century ago.
cards.move: The average is held at 100 by moving the goalposts every few years.

cards.question: Who were the experiments actually run on?
cards.answer: Overwhelmingly, undergraduates in rich Western universities — a group later shown to be among the least typical humans on measures from fairness to visual illusions. A field describing "human nature" had been sampling the most unusual population available, because it was the one down the corridor.
cards.move: The default human in psychology was a Western undergraduate.
cards.source: Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan, Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 2010
cards.reference: Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan, The weirdest people in the world?, Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 2010

cards.question: Does a confident witness mean a reliable one?
cards.answer: Only weakly — and confidence moves after the fact. Witnesses told they picked the right person become markedly more certain, and also recall a better view and a clearer memory. The confidence a jury hears in court has already been shaped by what happened after the identification.
cards.move: Confidence in the witness box is partly manufactured after the event.
cards.source: Wells & Bradfield, Journal of Applied Psychology, 1998
cards.reference: Wells & Bradfield, Good, you identified the suspect: feedback to eyewitnesses distorts their reports of the witnessing experience, Journal of Applied Psychology, 1998

cards.question: Do you know how a zip works?
cards.answer: Ask someone to rate their understanding of a zip, a toilet or a bicycle and they rate it high. Ask them to write the step-by-step mechanism and the rating collapses. We routinely mistake familiarity for understanding, and only notice when forced to produce the explanation.
cards.move: Try explaining how a zip works. Out loud. Right now.
cards.reference: Rozenblit & Keil, The misunderstood limits of folk science: an illusion of explanatory depth, Cognitive Science, 2002

cards.question: Would you notice if your own choice were swapped?
cards.answer: Often not. Shown two faces, asked to pick the more attractive, then handed back the other one and asked why — most people explain the choice they did not make, in detail, without noticing the swap. The reasons arrive after the decision and fit whatever is in front of us.
cards.move: People will argue confidently for a choice they never made.
cards.reference: Johansson, Hall, Sikström & Olsson, Failure to detect mismatches between intention and outcome in a simple decision task, Science, 2005

cards.question: Should schools sort pupils into classes by ability?
cards.answer: A single class spanning four years of attainment fails at both ends: the strongest coast, the weakest drown, and the teacher aims at a middle that nobody occupies. Grouping lets the material meet the pupil where they are, which is the one thing that reliably moves attainment.
cards.move: Ask what happens to the child placed in the bottom set by mistake, and how they would ever get out.
cards.counterpoint: The gains concentrate almost entirely in the top set, and the bottom set loses more than the top gains. Placement tracks family income as much as ability, gets made early, and rarely gets revisited — so a decision about a nine-year-old quietly becomes a decision about their adult life.
cards.reference: Education Endowment Foundation, Teaching and Learning Toolkit: Setting and streaming, 2021

cards.question: Should city centres have a default speed limit of 30 km/h?
cards.answer: The survival curve is not gradual: being struck at 50 kills a pedestrian far more often than being struck at 30, and city journeys are so dominated by junctions and lights that the lower limit costs almost no real time.
cards.move: Notice that one side is arguing about physics and the other about behaviour. Both can be right.
cards.counterpoint: Compliance is what actually determines speed, and a limit drivers regard as absurd gets ignored, which erodes the limits that matter. The same money spent on separating pedestrians from traffic saves more lives than a number on a sign.
cards.reference: Rosén & Sander, Pedestrian fatality risk as a function of car impact speed, Accident Analysis & Prevention, 2009

cards.question: How did we know what a kilogram was?
cards.answer: Until 2019, a kilogram was a metal cylinder in a vault near Paris. Its official copies drifted apart by around 50 micrograms over a century — and nobody could say which had changed, because the cylinder was the definition. It is now fixed to a constant of nature instead.
cards.move: For 130 years the kilogram could not be wrong, only different.
cards.reference: BIPM, The International System of Units (SI Brochure), 9th edition, 2019

cards.question: When did peer review become normal?
cards.answer: Later than you would guess. Nature only made external refereeing compulsory in 1973. Einstein's 1905 papers were not refereed, and neither was Watson and Crick's DNA structure. "Peer reviewed" describes a process younger than the polio vaccine, not a timeless standard.
cards.move: Peer review is younger than the polio vaccine.
cards.source: Baldwin, Notes and Records of the Royal Society, 2015
cards.reference: Baldwin, Credibility, peer review, and Nature, 1945-1990, Notes and Records of the Royal Society, 2015

cards.question: Where did the nitrogen in your body come from?
cards.answer: Roughly half of it passed through a factory. Air is 78% nitrogen that living things cannot use; the Haber-Bosch process forces it into fertiliser. That reaction now underwrites the food supply of about half the people alive, which makes it hard to name a more consequential chemistry.
cards.move: About half the nitrogen atoms in you came out of a chemical plant.

cards.question: Without relativity corrections, how far would a GPS satellite's clock drift from ground clocks each day?
cards.answer: About 38 microseconds. Weaker gravity 20,200 km up makes the satellite clock gain about 46 microseconds a day, and its orbital speed makes it lose about 7. Because positions come from light-travel times, 38 microseconds of error is roughly 11 km of drift in a single day.
cards.move: Multiply a small timing error by the speed of light before calling it small.
cards.trap: Assuming relativity only matters close to the speed of light.

cards.question: Should some research grants be handed out by lottery among the proposals that clear a quality bar?
cards.answer: Panels agree on which proposals are excellent and then cannot reliably separate the top slice from each other — re-scoring the same applications gives different winners. A lottery admits that honestly, costs a fraction of the reviewing effort, and stops rewarding whoever writes grants best rather than whoever does science best.
cards.move: Both sides accept the scoring is noisy. They disagree on whether noise is worse than no judgement at all.
cards.counterpoint: A draw removes the one moment where a field decides what matters most right now. Ranking is noisy, but it is not random, and the top of a good panel's list does outperform the middle. A lottery also strips accountability: nobody has to defend a bad allocation, because nobody made it.
cards.source: Trialled by the Health Research Council of New Zealand and the Volkswagen Foundation
cards.reference: Fang & Casadevall, Research Funding: the Case for a Modified Lottery, mBio, 2016

cards.question: Should we fund research into cooling the planet by putting particles in the stratosphere?
cards.answer: Not studying something does not stop it happening; it just guarantees that whoever tries it first will do so without knowing what follows. Research is not deployment, and the option value of understanding a lever we may be desperate for in forty years is very high.
cards.move: Research and deployment are separable in principle. The disagreement is whether they have ever been separated in practice.
cards.counterpoint: Every serious programme of this kind has ended in deployment, and the moral hazard is not hypothetical: the credible promise of a thermostat weakens the argument for cutting emissions today. It also hands one country a lever over everyone else's rainfall, with no mechanism to say no.
cards.reference: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, Reflecting Sunlight: Recommendations for Solar Geoengineering Research and Research Governance, 2021

cards.question: Why does the catalogue of known planets look so strange?
cards.answer: Almost every exoplanet was found either by the star wobbling or by the star dimming as the planet crosses it. Both work best on big planets orbiting close in. So the catalogue is not a census of planets — it is a census of the planets those two methods can see.
cards.move: The list of known planets is a list of what the instruments can detect.
cards.reference: Akeson et al., The NASA Exoplanet Archive: Data and Tools for Exoplanet Research, Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific, 2013

cards.question: What actually limits how far a probe can go?
cards.answer: Not physics — plutonium-238. Deep-space probes run on its heat because sunlight is too weak out there. The United States stopped making it in 1988, ran down its stock, and only restarted production in 2015. Missions were planned around the size of a shelf.
cards.move: The edge of the solar system is a supply-chain problem.
cards.source: US Department of Energy, Pu-238 supply programme
cards.reference: National Research Council, Radioisotope Power Systems: An Imperative for Maintaining U.S. Leadership in Space Exploration, National Academies Press, 2009

cards.question: Where does the atmosphere end?
cards.answer: Nowhere in particular. The Karman line at 100 km is a round number chosen for convenience, not a boundary in nature. There is still enough air well above it to drag satellites down, which is why the space station has to be pushed back up several times a year.
cards.move: The edge of space is an agreed convention, not a discovery.
cards.source: Federation Aeronautique Internationale; ISS reboost logs
cards.reference: McDowell, The edge of space: Revisiting the Karman Line, Acta Astronautica, 2018

cards.question: Where did most of the tracked space junk come from?
cards.answer: Two events. A 2007 anti-satellite test and a 2009 collision between a working satellite and a dead one together produced a large share of everything now catalogued in low orbit. The problem is not gradual litter; it is a handful of very bad days.
cards.move: Most of the debris up there came from two afternoons.
cards.reference: NASA Orbital Debris Program Office, Orbital Debris Quarterly News 13(2), 2009

cards.question: Is space really silent?
cards.answer: Sound needs a medium, and space has a thin one. Ripples through the gas of the Perseus galaxy cluster have been measured as pressure waves — a note about 57 octaves below middle C. Space is not silent so much as impossibly deep and impossibly quiet.
cards.move: There is a note in the Perseus cluster. Nobody could ever hear it.

cards.question: Where does the internet physically go?
cards.answer: Under the sea. Around 99% of intercontinental data travels through a few hundred fibre-optic cables lying on the seabed, not through satellites. "The cloud" is mostly glass on a seafloor, and its main hazards are ships' anchors and fishing trawlers.
cards.move: The cloud is a few hundred cables on the bottom of the ocean.

cards.question: Was QWERTY designed to slow you down?
cards.answer: Almost certainly not. The jamming story is folklore attached after the fact. The arrangement grew from how early machines were built and used — including telegraph operators transcribing Morse, who needed certain letters close together. It stuck because everyone had already learned it, which is the real lesson.
cards.move: The layout on your phone was settled by 1870s telegraph habits.
cards.reference: Yasuoka & Yasuoka, On the Prehistory of QWERTY, ZINBUN 42, Kyoto University, 2011

cards.question: Why can a helium shortage close a hospital?
cards.answer: MRI scanners need liquid helium to keep their magnets superconducting. Helium cannot be manufactured — it is collected as a by-product of certain natural gas wells, and it escapes Earth's gravity once released. Shortages have delayed scans and shut machines down.
cards.move: Helium is not made. It is found, used once, and lost to space.
cards.source: US Geological Survey, helium commodity summaries
cards.reference: US Geological Survey, Mineral Commodity Summaries: Helium, 2024

cards.question: What is the most software-heavy thing you own?
cards.answer: Probably your car. A modern vehicle runs on the order of a hundred million lines of code across dozens of processors — considerably more than a passenger aircraft. Most of it is not the engine; it is entertainment, comfort and the screens.
cards.move: Your car carries more code than the plane you flew in.

cards.question: Should courts use algorithmic risk scores when deciding bail?
cards.answer: The alternative to the algorithm is not neutrality, it is a tired judge before lunch. A score is at least consistent, auditable and testable — you can measure whether it is biased, which is more than anyone has ever been able to do to a bench.
cards.move: Auditable and fair are different properties. A model can be perfectly consistent about the wrong thing.
cards.counterpoint: A model trained on past arrests learns where police went, not where crime was, and then hands that pattern back wearing the authority of arithmetic. And the judge who follows it is answerable to nobody: the defendant cannot cross-examine a score, and the vendor will not release the weights.
cards.reference: Kleinberg, Lakkaraju, Leskovec, Ludwig & Mullainathan, Human Decisions and Machine Predictions, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2018

cards.question: Should an AI system be allowed to make a diagnosis without a doctor signing it off?
sides: No, keep a doctor in the loop
cards.answer: In several narrow tasks these systems already match specialists, and they do it at three in the morning in places with no specialist at all. Requiring a signature from someone who is not available is not a safety measure, it is a shortage dressed as one.
cards.move: The real question is not accuracy on average. It is what happens on the case that falls outside the training data.
cards.counterpoint: A doctor who signs off catches the case the model has never seen, and the model does not know which case that is. Add a rubber-stamping human and you get the worst of both: nobody actually checking, and nobody clearly responsible when it is wrong.
cards.reference: Topol, High-performance medicine: the convergence of human and artificial intelligence, Nature Medicine, 2019

cards.question: Should political advertising be banned from targeting narrow groups?
cards.answer: A promise made to eight thousand people that nobody else ever sees cannot be checked, contradicted or held against you. Broadcast advertising was accountable precisely because everyone saw the same claim — remove that and a campaign can tell every group a different story.
cards.move: Both sides are describing the same feature: reaching a few people cheaply.
cards.counterpoint: Targeting is also what lets a small campaign reach the people it is actually for, without buying national airtime. Ban it and the advantage returns to whoever can already afford to talk to everyone, which is the incumbent.
cards.reference: Information Commissioner's Office, Democracy disrupted? Personal information and political influence, 2018

cards.question: A school of 2,000 screens every pupil for a condition that affects 1 in 500. The screen catches 90% of cases and wrongly flags 5%. A child is flagged. Odds they have it?
cards.answer: Four children in 2,000 have it and the screen finds three or four of them. But 5% of the other 1,996 — about 100 children — are flagged too. Roughly 3 real cases against 100 false ones: under one flagged child in twenty actually has it.
cards.move: How rare the thing is matters more than how good the test is.
cards.trap: Reading 90% as the chance the flag is right.
cards.simply: Picture a village of 2,000. Four people are ill. The machine points at those four — and at about a hundred healthy people as well. When it points at you, look around: you are standing in a crowd of roughly a hundred, and four of you are ill.
cards.source: Base rate neglect in universal screening
cards.reference: Bar-Hillel, The base-rate fallacy in probability judgments, Acta Psychologica, 1980

cards.question: Marco is 45, cycles to work and reads a lot about climate. Which is more likely?
options: He owns a car and has solar panels
cards.answer: Every person with a car and panels also has a car, so the second group sits entirely inside the first and cannot be larger. Adding a detail that fits the story makes a claim feel likelier while making it strictly less likely.
cards.move: Adding detail makes a claim more convincing and less probable at the same time.
cards.trap: The second one fits the picture better, so it feels more probable.
cards.simply: Every dog wearing a hat is a dog. So there can never be more dogs-in-hats than there are dogs. However well the hat fits the story.
cards.reference: Tversky & Kahneman, Extensional versus intuitive reasoning: the conjunction fallacy in probability judgment, Psychological Review, 1983

cards.question: You are one of three finalists. A panel member privately tells you that one of the other two has been rejected. Have your chances improved?
cards.answer: They were always going to be able to name a rejected candidate among the other two, whoever wins — so hearing one name tells you nothing about you. Your one-in-three stands, and the remaining finalist now carries two-thirds.
cards.move: Information only moves the odds if it could have come out differently.
cards.trap: Two candidates left, so it feels like a coin flip.
cards.reference: Gardner, Mathematical Games, Scientific American, October 1959

cards.question: Order codes are generated at random from a million possibilities. After how many orders is a repeat more likely than not?
cards.answer: With n orders there are about n squared over two pairs that could clash, and a clash beats even odds once that count nears a million — around 1,200 orders. Collisions come from pairs, and pairs grow far faster than the list does.
cards.move: Coincidence needs far fewer people than anyone expects.
cards.trap: Thinking about your code, rather than every pair of codes.
cards.source: The birthday bound, applied to identifiers
cards.reference: Diaconis & Mosteller, Methods for Studying Coincidences, Journal of the American Statistical Association, 1989

cards.question: "Vintage tools were better made — every one I own still works." What is wrong?
options: The broken ones were thrown away decades ago
cards.answer: You are looking at what survived fifty years of use and disposal. The badly made ones broke and went in the bin long ago, so the tools left to buy are the durable tail of their generation — not a fair picture of what was on sale.
cards.move: Anything you can still buy from 1960 is, by definition, what did not break.
cards.trap: The surviving objects are treated as a sample of what was made.
cards.reference: Denrell, Vicarious Learning, Undersampling of Failure, and the Myths of Management, Organization Science, 2003

cards.question: You took a new remedy on the very worst day of a cold, and felt clearly better the next morning. What is the safest reading?
options: The worst day is usually followed by a better one
It works but only when you are very ill
cards.answer: You reach for a remedy when you feel worst, and the worst point of anything that fluctuates is usually followed by improvement whatever you do. That is why almost every treatment tried at the bottom appears to work.
cards.move: Anything you try at your worst moment will seem to help.
cards.trap: The improvement is real, so it feels like it needs a cause.
cards.source: Regression to the mean in self-treatment
cards.reference: Barnett, van der Pols & Dobson, Regression to the mean: what it is and how to deal with it, International Journal of Epidemiology, 2005

cards.question: Rule: anyone hired without a degree must have five years' experience. Four files: no degree / has degree / six years' experience / two years' experience. Which two must you open?
cards.answer: The no-degree file could break it, so open that. The two-years file could break it if that person has no degree, so open that. The degree file is not covered by the rule, and six years' experience can never break it — checking those two can only confirm what you already believe.
cards.move: Look for the file that could prove you wrong, not the one that agrees.
cards.trap: Checking the case that would confirm the rule rather than break it.
cards.source: The Wason selection task, in a hiring file
cards.reference: Wason, Reasoning about a rule, Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1968

cards.question: A delivery firm's on-time rate fell this year, although it improved in every single city it serves. Possible?
options: No, one of the numbers is wrong
Yes, if the mix of cities changed
cards.answer: If the firm grew fastest in its hardest cities, those now carry more weight in the total. Every city can improve while the overall average falls, because the average is over a different mix of deliveries than last year.
cards.move: A total and its parts can honestly point opposite ways.
cards.trap: Assuming the total has to move with its parts.
cards.simply: Two classes both got better at spelling this year. But the big struggling class grew and the small strong class shrank. The school's average went down. Everybody improved and the school looks worse.
cards.reference: Simpson, The Interpretation of Interaction in Contingency Tables, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B, 1951

cards.question: Buy three, get the cheapest free. The items cost €10, €20 and €30. What is the discount?
cards.answer: You pay €50 instead of €60, so you save a sixth. One item in three is free, which sounds like 33% — but it is the cheapest item, and it was never a third of the money.
cards.move: One item in three free is nothing like a third off.
cards.trap: The word "free" attaches to an item, not to the bill.
cards.reference: Paulos, Innumeracy: Mathematical Illiteracy and Its Consequences, Hill and Wang, 1988

cards.question: A landfill fills in 40 years at current waste growth of 7% a year. At 10% growth, roughly how much sooner?
cards.answer: About eight years. What fills a landfill is the running total. At 7% growth, forty years add up to about 200 years of today's waste; at 10% the same total piles up in about 32 years. Three points on the growth rate take a fifth off the landfill's life.
cards.move: Small changes in a growth rate are large changes in the total.
cards.trap: Treating a few extra percent as a small change.
cards.simply: A pile that doubles every ten years is nothing for ages and then swallows the room. Make it double every seven instead and you do not add a little — you lose a decade.
cards.reference: Bartlett, Forgotten Fundamentals of the Energy Crisis, American Journal of Physics, 1978

cards.question: A random quality check has passed 40 units in a row. Is the next more likely to fail?
options: Yes, the machine is warming up
cards.answer: If the checks really are independent, the line has no memory of the last 40. The run should make you ask a different question instead: whether the failure rate is lower than you assumed, or whether the check is actually testing anything.
cards.move: A run of luck does not owe you anything, but it might be telling you something else.
cards.trap: Feeling that a run has to even out.
cards.reference: Tversky & Kahneman, Belief in the law of small numbers, Psychological Bulletin, 1971

cards.question: A city has spent €400m of a planned €1bn tunnel. New figures show it will never repay its cost. What should decide whether to continue?
options: Only the remaining €600m against the benefit
cards.answer: The €400m is gone whichever way you choose, so it cannot favour either. The only live question is whether the remaining €600m buys more than €600m of anything else. Counting the spent money is how projects that everyone knows are failing get finished.
cards.move: The money already spent has no vote.
cards.trap: The spent money feels like it would be wasted by stopping.
cards.reference: Arkes & Blumer, The psychology of sunk cost, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 1985

cards.question: An estate agent shows you the most expensive house on the street first. Why?
options: Every later price is judged against it
cards.answer: The first number becomes the reference the rest are measured from, even when you know it was chosen to impress. The effect persists when people are warned about it, and when the anchor is plainly arbitrary.
cards.move: Whoever names the first number has already moved yours.
cards.trap: Believing your sense of a fair price is your own.
cards.reference: Tversky & Kahneman, Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases, Science, 1974

cards.question: After a widely reported plane crash, bookings fall and more people drive instead. What happens to total deaths?
options: They fall, flying is riskier for a while
They rise, because driving is more dangerous per kilometre
cards.answer: Road travel kills far more people per kilometre than flying. Measured after the 2001 attacks, the shift from planes to cars in the following months was estimated to have cost more American lives than were lost aboard the aircraft.
cards.move: The safest place after a plane crash is on a plane.
cards.trap: Fear tracks how vivid a risk is, not how large.
cards.reference: Gigerenzer, Out of the Frying Pan into the Fire: Behavioral Reactions to Terrorist Attacks, Risk Analysis, 2006

cards.question: A recruiter believes graduates of one university do better, so only interviews those. How could they ever discover they were wrong?
options: From the performance of who they hire
They could not — the test never runs
cards.answer: Everyone hired comes from that university, so every good hire confirms the rule and no rejected candidate ever gets to disprove it. The belief is not surviving tests; it is preventing them.
cards.move: Ask what result would have changed your mind. If none could, nothing is being tested.
cards.trap: A belief that keeps being confirmed feels like a belief that keeps being tested.
cards.reference: Nickerson, Confirmation Bias: A Ubiquitous Phenomenon in Many Guises, Review of General Psychology, 1998

cards.question: Judges were shown a sentencing demand rolled on dice before deciding a case. What happened?
options: Nothing — they are trained to ignore it
cards.answer: Experienced judges gave longer sentences after a high roll than a low one, knowing the number came from dice. Expertise does not remove the anchor; it makes people more certain they were not anchored.
cards.move: Whoever names a figure first has already moved the room, expert or not.
cards.trap: Assuming expertise protects against an irrelevant number.
cards.reference: Englich, Mussweiler & Strack, Playing Dice With Criminal Sentences, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 2006

cards.question: A shop marks an item "was €200, now €80". Why does the crossed-out price work even when it was never charged?
options: People assume it is a real discount
It sets the number you judge €80 against
cards.answer: The first figure becomes the reference point, and €80 is then read as a saving rather than as a price. It works on people who doubt the original price was ever real — which is why the practice is regulated rather than merely mocked.
cards.move: The crossed-out number is not information. It is the ruler.
cards.trap: Thinking the effect depends on believing the old price.
cards.reference: Tversky & Kahneman, Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases, Science, 1974

cards.question: A camera that identifies faces with 99% accuracy scans 100,000 travellers to find one wanted person. Roughly how many alarms will be wrong?
cards.answer: One per cent of 100,000 innocent people is about 1,000 false alarms, against the single real match. Almost every alarm is wrong — not because the camera is bad, but because there is only one of them and a hundred thousand of us.
cards.move: A very accurate test looking for something very rare is mostly wrong.
cards.trap: Hearing 99% and picturing a system that is almost always right.
cards.source: Base rate neglect applied to screening
cards.reference: Bar-Hillel, The base-rate fallacy in probability judgments, Acta Psychologica, 1980

cards.question: A hiring tool spots the 5% of applicants who become top performers, with 80% accuracy. You are flagged. What are your odds?
cards.answer: Of 1,000 applicants, 50 are top performers and 40 get flagged. But 20% of the other 950 get flagged too: 190 more. So about 40 of 230 flags are real — under one in five.
cards.move: Ask how rare the thing is before you ask how good the test is.
cards.trap: Reading the tool's accuracy as the chance it is right about you.
cards.reference: Bar-Hillel, The base-rate fallacy in probability judgments, Acta Psychologica, 1980

cards.question: You think a colleague dislikes you, and start noticing the evidence. Why does the evidence keep arriving?
options: Because you are only counting what fits
Because they can tell you suspect it
cards.answer: The neutral moments are not stored, so the pile can only grow one way. The test that would tell you something is looking for the times they went out of their way for you — and noticing whether you had been discounting them.
cards.move: A theory that only ever gains evidence is not being tested.
cards.trap: Treating a growing pile of confirming moments as proof.
cards.reference: Nickerson, Confirmation Bias: A Ubiquitous Phenomenon in Many Guises, Review of General Psychology, 1998

cards.question: Should social media have a legal minimum age of 16?
cards.answer: A minimum age treats a designed-to-be-addictive product the way we treat alcohol and gambling. Parents cannot realistically opt one child out of where every classmate lives, so the choice is not free in practice — a floor removes that trap for everyone at once.
cards.move: Whichever side you took, the enforcement question is the one that decides it.
cards.counterpoint: Bans push teenagers to lie about their age rather than stay off, which makes them less visible and less protected. Enforcement means verifying identity for everyone, handing platforms more personal data than they hold now. And the evidence on harm is contested — much of it is correlational, and the effect sizes found are often small.
cards.reference: Orben & Przybylski, The association between adolescent well-being and digital technology use, Nature Human Behaviour, 2019

cards.question: A self-driving car must choose: swerve and kill one, or continue and kill five. What should it be built to do?
cards.answer: A machine should do what a clear-headed person would want in advance, and almost nobody, asked in the abstract, prefers five deaths to one. Building anything else means writing a rule that some lives count less because of where they are standing.
cards.move: The gap between what people say they want and what they would buy is the whole problem.
cards.counterpoint: People say they want the car to minimise deaths, and then say they would not buy that car. A vehicle that might sacrifice its passenger will not sell, so the ethical version never reaches the road and the far larger benefit — fewer crashes overall — never arrives.
cards.reference: Bonnefon, Shariff & Rahwan, The social dilemma of autonomous vehicles, Science, 2016

cards.question: Should people be paid for donating a kidney?
cards.answer: People die on waiting lists while healthy kidneys go undonated. Iran, the one country with a regulated payment system, reported its kidney waiting list cleared by 1999. We already pay surgeons, nurses and hospitals — the only person forbidden to benefit is the one taking the risk.
cards.move: Both sides agree people are dying. They disagree about what counts as a free choice.
cards.counterpoint: A price makes the poor the supply. If the offer is life-changing money, refusing stops being a free choice, and the burden of organ removal lands almost entirely on people with no other options. Consent given under financial pressure is the thing the rule exists to protect.
cards.reference: Ghods & Savaj, Iranian Model of Paid and Regulated Living-Unrelated Kidney Donation, Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology, 2006

cards.question: Should we bring back extinct species we have the technology to revive?
cards.answer: We caused most of these extinctions, and restoring a lost species can repair an ecosystem that lost its engineer. The techniques developed also help species that are still alive but failing.
cards.move: The strongest objection is not scientific. It is what the promise does to the incentive.
cards.counterpoint: The money is finite, and it competes directly with protecting species that still exist. A revived animal returns to a habitat that has moved on without it, and the promise of reversal weakens the argument for not causing extinctions in the first place.
cards.reference: Bennett et al., Spending limited resources on de-extinction could lead to net biodiversity loss, Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2017

cards.question: How many tonnes of coffee does Italy drink in a year, in thousands of tonnes?
cards.answer: x 365 = ~300,000 tonnes. The reported figure is around 370,000.
cards.move: Two espressos a day, times a country, is a third of a million tonnes.
cards.hint: Start from cups per person per day and the grams in a cup.
steps: About 59 million people, and roughly 2 servings a day on average across everyone.
An espresso uses about 7 g, so ~14 g per person per day.
14 g x 59 million = ~830 tonnes a day.
x 365 = ~300,000 tonnes. The reported figure is around 370,000.
cards.reference: International Coffee Organization, domestic consumption statistics, 2019

cards.question: How many bricks are in a typical four-storey apartment building, in thousands?
cards.answer: 2,500 x 60 = ~150,000. With party walls and returns, a few hundred thousand.
cards.move: The building you live in is a quarter of a million bricks somebody laid by hand.
cards.hint: Work out the wall area, then bricks per square metre.
steps: A brick face is about 21 x 6 cm with mortar, so ~60 bricks per square metre per leaf.
A 20 m x 12 m building, 12 m tall: perimeter 64 m x 12 m = ~770 square metres of wall.
Two leaves and internal walls, call it ~2,500 square metres of brickwork.
2,500 x 60 = ~150,000. With party walls and returns, a few hundred thousand.
cards.reference: BS 3921:1985, Specification for clay bricks

cards.question: How many words does a person speak in a day?
cards.move: Men and women came out within a few hundred words of each other when it was measured.
cards.hint: Speaking runs at roughly 130 words a minute; the question is how many minutes.
steps: Recorded speech runs about 130 words per minute.
People actually speak for perhaps 2 hours of a waking day.
cards.reference: Mehl, Vazire, Ramírez-Esparza, Slatcher & Pennebaker, Are Women Really More Talkative Than Men?, Science, 2007

cards.question: How many passenger journeys does one city bus make in its working life, in millions?
cards.answer: A bus serves 12 to 15 years: ~1.7 million boardings.
cards.move: One bus moves more people in its life than live in Milan.
cards.hint: Journeys per day, times days per year, times years of service.
steps: A busy city bus carries roughly 400 boardings a day.
It runs around 320 days a year: ~128,000 a year.
A bus serves 12 to 15 years: ~1.7 million boardings.
cards.reference: Department for Transport, Annual bus statistics: England, 2019

cards.question: How many hours of video are uploaded to the world's video platforms every minute, in thousands?
cards.answer: That is more than a month of footage produced every minute.
cards.move: More video is uploaded each minute than one person could watch in a month.
cards.hint: You only need the order of magnitude, not the exact platform figures.
steps: Reported uploads to the largest platform alone run to several hundred hours a minute.
Adding the rest brings it to the order of a thousand hours per minute.
That is more than a month of footage produced every minute.
cards.reference: YouTube, press statistics: 500 hours of video uploaded every minute, 2019

cards.question: "Every successful founder I interviewed woke at 5am. So waking early makes you successful." Where does this break?
options: Waking early is not that helpful
Nobody asked the founders who failed
Five is too early to be realistic
cards.answer: The sample was chosen by its outcome. If half of all failed founders also woke at 5am, the habit tells you nothing. You cannot learn what causes success by studying only successes.
cards.move: Ask who is missing from the sample before you argue about the finding.
cards.trap: Arguing about whether waking early works, instead of about the sample.
cards.reference: Denrell, Vicarious Learning, Undersampling of Failure, and the Myths of Management, Organization Science, 2003

cards.question: "Hospitals are dangerous: far more people die in them than at home." What is wrong?
options: The figures are probably made up
People go to hospital because they are already dying
cards.answer: The comparison assumes the two groups are alike, and they are not: hospitals concentrate the sickest people. Judging a treatment needs comparable groups, which is what a control group is for.
cards.move: Any statistic comparing two groups invites one question: who ended up in each?
cards.trap: Treating a place where sick people are sent as a cause of their outcome.
cards.reference: Kyriacou & Lewis, Confounding by Indication in Clinical Research, JAMA, 2016

cards.question: "After the new mayor, crime fell 8%. The policy worked." What is missing?
options: Eight percent is too small to matter
What crime did everywhere else over the same period
cards.answer: If crime fell 12% nationally, this mayor did worse than doing nothing. A number with no comparison group cannot support a claim about cause — that is what a counterfactual is for.
cards.move: "Compared to what?" is the most useful question in any argument.
cards.trap: Judging a change without anything to compare it against.
cards.reference: Holland, Statistics and Causal Inference, Journal of the American Statistical Association, 1986

cards.question: A study tests 20 foods against cancer risk and finds one significant at p < 0.05. What should you think?
options: Convincing — that is the standard threshold
Expected by chance: 20 tests, 1 in 20 odds
They should have tested more foods
cards.answer: A 5% threshold means one false positive in twenty tests on average. Run twenty tests and finding one "result" is what should happen if nothing is going on. The fix is to say up front what you are testing.
cards.move: Ask how many things they measured before you believe the one they report.
cards.trap: Reading a single p-value without asking how many tests were run.
cards.reference: Ioannidis, Why Most Published Research Findings Are False, PLOS Medicine, 2005

cards.question: "Nobody I know voted for it, so the result must be rigged." Where is the error?
options: They probably did not check carefully
The people you know are not a random sample
One election is too small a sample
cards.answer: People cluster with people like themselves, so your circle is one of the least random samples available. Pauline Kael is often misquoted saying this about Nixon; the underlying error is real regardless.
cards.move: Your social circle is evidence about your social circle.
cards.trap: Treating the people around you as if they were drawn at random.
cards.reference: Squire, Why the 1936 Literary Digest Poll Failed, Public Opinion Quarterly, 1988

cards.question: A survey is emailed to customers and 4% reply, overwhelmingly positive. What has it measured?
options: The views of people who still open your email
cards.answer: A small random sample would be fine. This one is not random: it excludes everyone who has stopped opening your email, which is exactly the unhappy. The size is not the problem — who is missing is.
cards.move: The people who did not answer are the finding.
cards.trap: Reading a low response rate as merely a small sample.
cards.reference: Groves, Nonresponse Rates and Nonresponse Bias in Household Surveys, Public Opinion Quarterly, 2006

cards.question: Online ratings for most products cluster at five stars and one star, with little between. Why?
options: Products really are either great or terrible
Only the delighted and the furious bother to write
cards.answer: Writing a review costs effort, and only strong feeling pays for it. The many people who found it fine never appear, so the distribution is about who writes, not about what the product is like.
cards.move: The middle of any rating scale is missing, not empty.
cards.trap: Reading the shape of the ratings as the shape of the experience.
cards.reference: Hu, Pavlou & Zhang, Overcoming the J-shaped distribution of product reviews, Communications of the ACM, 2009

cards.question: A cyclist rides 6 km uphill at 10 km/h and straight back down at 30 km/h. What is the average speed, in km/h?
cards.answer: 12 km in 0.8 hours is 15 km/h.
cards.move: Average the times, not the speeds, when the distance is fixed.
cards.trap: Averaging 10 and 30, because both legs cover the same distance.
cards.hint: Work out how long each half takes, not how fast it is.
steps: Uphill: 6 / 10 = 0.6 hours.
Downhill: 6 / 30 = 0.2 hours.
12 km in 0.8 hours is 15 km/h.
cards.reference: Paulos, Innumeracy: Mathematical Illiteracy and Its Consequences, Hill and Wang, 1988

cards.question: A magnitude 8 earthquake against a magnitude 6: how much more energy does the bigger one release?
cards.answer: About 1,000 times. Each whole step on the magnitude scale is ten times the shaking recorded and about 32 times the energy, so two steps are roughly 32 × 32. A magnitude 8 releases in one event what a thousand magnitude 6 quakes would.
cards.move: On a scale that counts powers, one step is never one step.
cards.trap: Knowing each step is ten times, and stopping at the shaking.
cards.reference: Kanamori, The energy release in great earthquakes, Journal of Geophysical Research, 1977

cards.question: Driving 10,000 km a year, which upgrade saves more fuel: 5 to 10 km per litre, or 20 to 40?
cards.answer: 5 to 10. At 5 km per litre the year takes 2,000 litres and at 10 it takes 1,000: a saving of 1,000. Going from 20 to 40 cuts 500 litres to 250: a saving of 250. Both double, but one doubling starts from a far thirstier engine.
cards.move: Judge an improvement by what it saves, not by its ratio.
cards.trap: Both are doublings, and the bigger numbers look like the bigger gain.
cards.reference: Larrick & Soll, The MPG Illusion, Science, 2008

cards.question: A pill cuts a disease's yearly risk from 2 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000. How many must take it to spare one person?
cards.answer: About 1,000. The pill halves the risk, but the risk was 2 in 1,000 to begin with, so it removes one case per 1,000 people a year. Doctors call this the number needed to treat. The same halving on a 1-in-2 risk would spare one person in four.
cards.move: Ask what a halving is a halving of before you are impressed.
cards.trap: Hearing that the pill halves the risk and picturing half the patients saved.
cards.reference: Laupacis, Sackett & Roberts, An assessment of clinically useful measures of the consequences of treatment, New England Journal of Medicine, 1988

cards.question: True or false: a shop that prices goods at cost plus 50% keeps half of each sale as margin?
cards.answer: False. Buy at €100 and sell at €150, and the €50 kept is a third of the price, not half. Markup is measured on the cost and margin on the sale, so the same €50 is 50% one way and 33% the other.
cards.move: Name the base of every percentage before you compare two of them.
cards.trap: Reading fifty per cent on the cost as fifty per cent of the price.
cards.reference: Paulos, Innumeracy: Mathematical Illiteracy and Its Consequences, Hill and Wang, 1988

cards.question: A rope hugs the equator. Add 1 m to its length and raise it evenly all round. Can a cat crawl under?
options: Yes, the gap is about 16 cm
Barely, the gap is about 1 mm
cards.answer: Yes, easily. A circle's circumference is 2π times its radius, so adding 1 m to the rope lifts it by 1 ÷ 2π, about 16 cm, all the way round — whatever the size of the circle. The same extra metre around a football would lift it by the same 16 cm.
cards.move: When the intuition comes from size, check whether size appears in the formula.
cards.trap: One metre spread over 40,000 km feels like nothing at all.
cards.source: Circumference and radius of a circle
cards.reference: Courant & Robbins, What Is Mathematics?, revised by Stewart, Oxford University Press, 1996

cards.question: A launch needs five independent steps done on time, each 90% likely. How likely is an on-time launch?
cards.answer: About 60%. Every step must succeed, so the chances multiply: 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 is 0.59. Each step looks safe on its own, and the plan still fails two times in five. Ten such steps would fail more often than they succeed.
cards.move: Multiply the odds of every step a plan needs before trusting it.
cards.trap: Each step is safe, so the whole plan feels safe.
cards.reference: Tversky & Kahneman, Extensional versus intuitive reasoning: the conjunction fallacy in probability judgment, Psychological Review, 1983

cards.question: A new café opens on your street, with a gifted barista. Which is more likely?
options: It wins an award and survives three years
cards.answer: Surviving three years. Every café that wins an award and survives is also a café that survives, so the second can never be the likelier. The award supplies a reason, and a reason makes a story feel probable while cutting down the number of ways it can come true.
cards.move: Each added reason is one more thing that has to be true.
cards.trap: The award explains the survival, so the story feels more likely.
cards.source: Conjunction rule, applied to a forecast
cards.reference: Tversky & Kahneman, Extensional versus intuitive reasoning: the conjunction fallacy in probability judgment, Psychological Review, 1983

cards.question: True or false: a team with a 70% chance of winning each of its last four matches will probably win all four?
cards.answer: False. Each win has to happen, so the chances multiply: 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.7 is about 0.24. A team that is favourite in every single match still has only about one chance in four of winning the lot.
cards.move: Being favourite at every step is not being favourite for the journey.
cards.trap: Favourite in every match feels like favourite for the whole run.
cards.reference: Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Volume 1, Wiley, 1968

cards.question: A €1,000 card debt grows at 2% a month, unpaid, for three years. Roughly what is owed?
cards.answer: About €2,040. Each month's 2% is charged on the interest already added, so the debt multiplies by 1.02 thirty-six times, which is a little over 2. Simple interest would give €1,720: the gap is interest on interest, and it widens every month.
cards.move: Turn a monthly rate into a yearly one before deciding it is small.
cards.trap: Adding 2% thirty-six times instead of multiplying by it.
cards.reference: Bartlett, Forgotten Fundamentals of the Energy Crisis, American Journal of Physics, 1978

cards.question: A drug's level in the blood halves every 6 hours. After a 400 mg dose, how many mg remain a day later?
cards.answer: 25 mg remain after a day.
cards.move: What halves never reaches zero; count the halvings, not the amount lost.
cards.trap: Taking off a fixed 100 mg every six hours, as if steady.
cards.hint: Count how many six-hour halvings fit in a day.
steps: A day is 24 / 6 = 4 half-lives.
400 halved four times: 200, 100, 50, 25.
25 mg remain after a day.
cards.reference: Rowland & Tozer, Clinical Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics, Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2011

cards.question: True or false: most crashes happen within a few kilometres of home, so driving near home is riskier?
cards.answer: False. Most crashes happen near home because most driving happens near home. The share of crashes in a place says where people drive, not how dangerous each kilometre there is. To compare risk, divide the crashes by the kilometres driven in each place.
cards.move: Where most accidents happen is mostly where most people are.
cards.trap: Reading the share of crashes as the danger of the place.
cards.reference: Evans, Traffic Safety, Science Serving Society, 2004

cards.question: Two friends each roll a die in secret. You ask whether either rolled a six; they say yes. Chance both did?
cards.answer: 1 in 11. Of the 36 equally likely pairs, 11 contain at least one six, and only one of those is a double six. The yes ruled out the 25 pairs without a six, but it did not tell you which die showed it, so the other die is not a fresh roll.
cards.move: Ask exactly what you were told, and which cases it rules out.
cards.trap: One die shows a six, so the other feels like a fresh roll.
cards.reference: Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Volume 1, Wiley, 1968

cards.question: Ana outshoots Bea from close range and from long range, yet Bea has the better overall percentage. Possible?
options: No, the figures must be wrong
Yes, if Bea takes more close shots
Only if they played different games
cards.answer: Yes. Close shots go in far more often than long ones. If most of Bea's attempts are close and most of Ana's are long, Bea's total is weighted towards easy shots and beats Ana's, although Ana is better at each kind. The total measures the shot mix as much as the shooter.
cards.move: A total is a weighted average; ask who chose the weights.
cards.trap: Assuming someone better at every part must be better overall.
cards.reference: Wagner, Simpson's Paradox in Real Life, The American Statistician, 1982

cards.question: True or false: the share of income paid in tax can rise even if every income bracket's rate falls?
