cards.answer: True. It happened in the United States between 1974 and 1978: the average rate fell within every income bracket, yet the overall rate rose, because inflation pushed more of the country's income into the higher brackets, where rates were steepest. The mix moved faster than the rates.
cards.move: A shift in the mix can outrun a change in every part.
cards.trap: If every part goes down, the whole must go down too.
cards.reference: Wagner, Simpson's Paradox in Real Life, The American Statistician, 1982

cards.question: Two weather services, working from the same satellite data, both give a 70% chance of rain. How sure should you be?
cards.answer: Not much more than 70%. Combining forecasts sharpens the odds only when their errors are independent. Two services reading the same satellites through similar models share their mistakes, so their agreement is close to one forecast repeated. The 91% would need them to be wrong for different reasons.
cards.move: Agreement counts only as often as the sources could have disagreed.
cards.trap: Treating two agreeing sources as two separate pieces of evidence.
cards.reference: Clemen, Combining forecasts: A review and annotated bibliography, International Journal of Forecasting, 1989

cards.question: Three years into a law degree, you realise you want to be an engineer. What should those three years count for?
options: Only what they give you from now on
cards.answer: Only what they give you from now on. The years are spent whichever way you choose; what still counts is what they carry forward — skills, a qualification, contacts — weighed against the years an unwanted career would take. Finishing to avoid wasting them spends more years to protect ones already gone.
cards.move: The past votes only through what it hands to the future.
cards.trap: Stopping now feels like throwing three years away.
cards.reference: Arkes & Blumer, The psychology of sunk cost, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 1985

cards.question: In the European Union, which kills more people each year: air pollution or road crashes?
options: Air pollution, by over ten times
cards.answer: Air pollution, by more than ten times. Road crashes kill about 20,000 people a year across the European Union; fine-particle pollution is estimated to cause well over 200,000 early deaths. A crash is an event with a name and a place. A pollution death is recorded as a stroke or a heart attack.
cards.move: The risks you can photograph are rarely the ones doing the killing.
cards.trap: Crashes are named events; pollution deaths are filed under other causes.
cards.source: Lelieveld et al., European Heart Journal, 2019
cards.reference: Lelieveld et al., Cardiovascular disease burden from ambient air pollution in Europe reassessed using novel hazard ratio functions, European Heart Journal, 2019

cards.question: In 2009 Bulgaria's lottery drew the same six numbers in two draws running. What does that suggest?
cards.answer: Nothing by itself. One draw matching the one before has odds of about one in 5 million, but hundreds of lotteries have run many draws a year for decades, so a repeat somewhere was due. Bulgaria investigated and found no wrongdoing.
cards.move: Before calling something a miracle, count everywhere it could have happened.
cards.trap: Judging the odds of this draw, not of any draw anywhere.
cards.reference: Hand, The Improbability Principle, Scientific American / Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2014

cards.question: True or false: pupils with the worst mock-exam marks will, on average, do better in the real exam even without extra help?
cards.answer: True. A mark is part ability and part luck on the day, and the lowest marks collect the worst luck. On the next test the luck is drawn again, so the group drifts back towards its average — which is why extra lessons aimed at them look effective even when they are not.
cards.move: Part of every score is luck, and luck is not repeated on demand.
cards.trap: Low marks feel like low ability, which should not move by itself.
cards.reference: Barnett, van der Pols & Dobson, Regression to the mean: what it is and how to deal with it, International Journal of Epidemiology, 2005

cards.question: After a month with a sleep app, 70% of users say they sleep better. What is the missing number?
options: How a similar group without it slept
How long the users slept before
cards.answer: How a similar group without the app slept. People install a sleep app in a bad patch, and bad patches mostly pass; the attention alone can help too. Only a comparison group shows how much of the 70% the app itself did, and it may be very little.
cards.move: An improvement needs a twin who got nothing before it counts as an effect.
cards.trap: A before-and-after with nobody who went without.
cards.reference: Holland, Statistics and Causal Inference, Journal of the American Statistical Association, 1986

cards.question: A manager has hired three people from the same university and now feels they should pick elsewhere. Is that reasoning sound?
options: Not as stated — the past hires do not change this candidate
Yes, three is already too many
cards.answer: There may be a real case for varied backgrounds, but that case does not come from the run. As stated, the manager is treating independent decisions as though the earlier ones changed the odds of the next — the same move as expecting tails after four heads.
cards.move: A good reason for a decision is not the same as the feeling that produced it.
cards.trap: Feeling that a run has to be balanced out.
cards.reference: Tversky & Kahneman, Belief in the law of small numbers, Psychological Bulletin, 1971

cards.question: A factory changes supplier and defects drop 12%. What would make this convincing?
options: Knowing what defects did on the lines that did not change
cards.answer: If defects fell 15% everywhere that quarter, the new supplier did worse than doing nothing. A number with no comparison cannot support a claim about cause, however large it is.
cards.move: "Compared to what" beats any figure quoted on its own.
cards.trap: Judging a change with nothing to compare it to.
cards.reference: Holland, Statistics and Causal Inference, Journal of the American Statistical Association, 1986

cards.question: A team tests 15 versions of a button and one beats the original at p < 0.05. What should they do?
options: Run that one again on its own
cards.answer: With 15 tests, a false winner at the 5% threshold is more likely than not. The number means something only for a test decided in advance, so the finding has to survive being the only thing you are looking at.
cards.move: The winner of a search is not the same as the winner of a test.
cards.trap: Treating the winner of many tests like the winner of one.
cards.reference: Kohavi, Tang & Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments, Cambridge University Press, 2020

cards.question: "The campaign did not work overall, but it worked for women aged 25-34 in the north." What is the risk?
options: The segment was found by looking, not chosen first
It probably works for other segments too
cards.answer: Cut any dataset enough ways and some slice will look like a success by chance alone. A subgroup named before the data was collected is evidence; one found afterwards is a hypothesis, and needs its own test.
cards.move: A result found by slicing has to survive being predicted.
cards.trap: Accepting a slice as a finding because the numbers in it are real.
cards.reference: Sun, Briel, Walter & Guyatt, Is a subgroup effect believable? Updating criteria to evaluate the credibility of subgroup analyses, BMJ, 2010

cards.question: A lift serves floors 1 to 20. How many different journeys are there from a lower floor to a higher one?
cards.move: Every "how many pairs" question is the same question wearing a costume.
cards.hint: Every journey is just a pair of floors, and the lower one comes first.
steps: Choose any two of the 20 floors: 20 x 19 = 380 ordered pairs.
Each unordered pair gives exactly one upward journey, so halve it.
cards.reference: Graham, Knuth & Patashnik, Concrete Mathematics, Addison-Wesley, 1994

cards.question: A league of 12 teams plays every other team twice. How many matches in a season?
cards.answer: Each pair plays twice: 66 x 2 = 132.
cards.move: Rounds in a league grow with the square of the teams, not the teams.
cards.hint: First count each pairing once, then remember they meet twice.
steps: Pairings: 12 x 11 / 2 = 66.
Each pair plays twice: 66 x 2 = 132.
cards.reference: Graham, Knuth & Patashnik, Concrete Mathematics, Addison-Wesley, 1994

cards.question: A hedge grows 60 cm each summer and is cut back 40 cm each winter. It starts at 2 m. In which summer does it first reach 5 m?
cards.answer: So the 13th summer takes it to 5 m.
cards.move: The last step is bigger than all the ones before it.
cards.hint: It only keeps 20 cm a year — except in the summer it finally gets there.
steps: Each full year, summer then winter, adds 60 - 40 = 20 cm.
To reach 5 m during a summer it must start that summer at 5.00 - 0.60 = 4.40 m.
From 2.00 m to 4.40 m takes (4.40 - 2.00) / 0.20 = 12 full years.
So the 13th summer takes it to 5 m.
cards.reference: Paulos, Innumeracy: Mathematical Illiteracy and Its Consequences, Hill and Wang, 1988

cards.question: A door code is 4 different letters from the 26-letter alphabet, order mattering. How many codes?
cards.move: Forbidding repeats barely dents the count. It is still a third of a million.
cards.hint: Each position has one fewer letter available than the last.
steps: 26 choices, then 25, then 24, then 23.
cards.reference: Graham, Knuth & Patashnik, Concrete Mathematics, Addison-Wesley, 1994

cards.question: You start with €1 and double it every day. On which day do you first pass €1,000,000?
cards.answer: 2^20 = 1,048,576, so day 21 passes it.
cards.move: Three weeks of doubling turns one euro into a million.
cards.hint: Doubling ten times multiplies by about a thousand.
steps: Day 1 is €1, so on day n you have 2^(n-1).
2^19 = 524,288 — day 20 is still under a million.
2^20 = 1,048,576, so day 21 passes it.
cards.reference: Bartlett, Forgotten Fundamentals of the Energy Crisis, American Journal of Physics, 1978

cards.question: Two bus routes leave the same stop every 12 and every 18 minutes, together at 6am. How many minutes until they leave together again?
cards.answer: The least common multiple takes the highest power of each: 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 = 36.
cards.move: Coincidences repeat on the least common multiple, never sooner.
cards.hint: You want the first time that is a whole number of both intervals.
steps: The least common multiple takes the highest power of each: 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 = 36.
cards.reference: Hardy & Wright, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers, Oxford University Press, 2008

cards.question: A shop raises a price by 10%, then advertises 10% off. Where are you?
options: One per cent below the old price
cards.answer: Take €100: up 10% is €110, then 10% off €110 is €99. The rises and the falls are percentages of different numbers, so they never cancel. The same asymmetry is why a 50% loss needs a 100% gain to undo.
cards.move: A percentage is always a percentage of something, and the something changes.
cards.trap: Cancelling the two tens, because they look like the same ten.
cards.reference: Frederick, Cognitive Reflection and Decision Making, Journal of Economic Perspectives, 2005

cards.question: A company sends consultants to its worst-performing sales region. Next quarter it improves. What is the safest reading?
options: Some of it would have happened anyway
cards.answer: A region is picked because it had an unusually bad quarter, and unusual results are partly luck. The next quarter drifts back toward that region's own average whatever anyone does. Without a comparable region left alone, you cannot tell the treatment from the drift.
cards.move: Anything chosen for being extreme will look improved next time.
cards.trap: Crediting the intervention with the whole improvement.
cards.source: Regression to the mean in management
cards.reference: Barnett, van der Pols & Dobson, Regression to the mean: what it is and how to deal with it, International Journal of Epidemiology, 2005

cards.question: "Old buildings were built to last — look how many are still standing." What is wrong with this?
options: The badly built ones already fell down
Old buildings are repaired more often
cards.answer: Every era built badly and well. Only the well-built survive to be admired, so any century looks like a golden age from far enough away. The comparison you want is against everything built then, most of which is gone.
cards.move: Every past era looks well made, because the bad parts are not there to see.
cards.trap: Judging a period by what is left of it.
cards.source: Survivorship bias in the built environment
cards.reference: Denrell, Vicarious Learning, Undersampling of Failure, and the Myths of Management, Organization Science, 2003

cards.question: A fund family advertises the ten-year returns of its funds. Why is the average flattering?
options: The funds that did badly were closed and left the table
cards.answer: Poor funds get merged away or shut, and their records leave with them. What remains is the survivors, so the family average describes a group selected for having done well. Regulators require some disclosure of this precisely because it flatters so reliably.
cards.move: Any performance table is a list of the ones still allowed to be on it.
cards.trap: Assuming the table lists every fund they ever ran.
cards.reference: Brown, Goetzmann, Ibbotson & Ross, Survivorship Bias in Performance Studies, Review of Financial Studies, 1992

cards.question: You paid for a year of a service and stopped using it after two months. Should the year you paid for keep you subscribed?
options: No, the year is gone either way
cards.answer: The payment is the same whether you use it or not, so it cannot inform the choice. The only live question is whether the next ten months are worth your attention — and annual pricing exists partly because that reasoning is so hard to apply.
cards.move: You cannot get money back by spending time on top of it.
cards.trap: Staying to redeem money that is already spent.
cards.reference: Arkes & Blumer, The psychology of sunk cost, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 1985

cards.question: Which takes more lives worldwide each year?
cards.answer: Suicide, by about half as many again: roughly 700,000 deaths a year worldwide against about 460,000 homicides. One is covered constantly and the other rarely, and coverage is what makes a cause of death feel common.
cards.move: What you can recall easily is a fact about the news, not about the world.
cards.trap: Reaching for the one that gets reported.
cards.reference: WHO, Suicide worldwide in 2019: Global Health Estimates, 2021; UNODC, Global Study on Homicide, 2023

cards.question: In a country of 60 million, how often should a genuine one-in-a-million-per-day event happen?
cards.answer: One in a million per person per day, across 60 million people, is 60 occurrences a day. Astonishing coincidences are guaranteed at scale — which is why a coincidence needs to be surprising *given how many chances there were*.
cards.move: With enough people, the miraculous is scheduled.
cards.trap: Hearing "one in a million" as "essentially impossible".
cards.reference: Diaconis & Mosteller, Methods for Studying Coincidences, Journal of the American Statistical Association, 1989

cards.question: Employees who use the company gym take fewer sick days. Should the company expand the gym?
options: Not on this evidence: healthy people use gyms
Only if the gym is free
cards.answer: Nobody assigned people to the gym; they chose. Whatever makes someone a gym user — health, age, energy, a job with slack in it — also affects sick days. The gym could do nothing and the figures would look the same.
cards.move: When people chose their own group, the groups differ before you do anything.
cards.trap: Reading a difference between two self-selected groups as an effect.
cards.reference: Shrank, Patrick & Brookhart, Healthy User and Related Biases in Observational Studies of Preventive Interventions, Journal of General Internal Medicine, 2011

cards.question: Children who take music lessons do better at school. What does this establish?
options: Music and maths use the same skills
cards.answer: Music lessons cost money and stable time, which travel with a great deal else. Randomised studies of music training find much smaller effects on school attainment than the correlation suggests — the gap between the two is the confounding.
cards.move: Ask what else comes with the thing before you credit the thing.
cards.trap: Accepting an appealing cause because the correlation is real.
cards.reference: Sala & Gobet, Does Far Transfer Exist? Negative Evidence From Chess, Music, and Working Memory Training, Current Directions in Psychological Science, 2017

cards.question: An insurer flags 2% of claims as suspicious. About 1 claim in 400 is actually fraudulent, and the flag catches most of those. Your claim is flagged. Odds it is fraud?
cards.answer: In 40,000 claims, 100 are fraud and the flag catches most — say 80. But 2% of 40,000 is 800 flags. Eighty real against 800 raised: roughly one flagged claim in ten is fraud, and nine honest people get a letter.
cards.move: A flag on a rare thing is mostly a flag on an ordinary one.
cards.trap: The flag feels like an accusation, so it feels like evidence.
cards.source: Base rate neglect in claims screening
cards.reference: Bar-Hillel, The base-rate fallacy in probability judgments, Acta Psychologica, 1980

cards.question: A sport tests every athlete for a drug perhaps 1 in 1,000 uses. The test is right 99% of the time. An athlete tests positive. What is the honest headline?
cards.answer: Among 10,000 athletes, 10 use it and about 10 test positive. But 1% of the other 9,990 — around 100 — test positive too. Roughly nine in ten positives are clean athletes, which is exactly why a second independent test exists.
cards.move: One test on a rare thing is a reason to test again, not a verdict.
cards.trap: Ninety-nine per cent sounds like near-certainty about the person.
cards.reference: Bar-Hillel, The base-rate fallacy in probability judgments, Acta Psychologica, 1980

cards.question: A factory sensor flags machines likely to fail this week. Failures are rare; the sensor is usually right. Most flags turn out to be nothing. Is the sensor broken?
options: No, that is what a rare event looks like
cards.answer: When the thing being looked for almost never happens, even a good detector produces mostly false alarms — there is simply far more of everything else. The number worth watching is how many real failures it misses, not how many alarms are quiet.
cards.move: Judge a detector by what it misses, not by how often it cries wolf.
cards.trap: Judging a detector by how often its alarms are real.
cards.source: Precision and recall on rare events
cards.reference: Saito & Rehmsmeier, The Precision-Recall Plot Is More Informative than the ROC Plot When Evaluating Binary Classifiers on Imbalanced Datasets, PLOS ONE, 2015

cards.question: "Films were better in the seventies." What is wrong with the comparison?
options: The bad ones from then are not screened any more
cards.answer: Hundreds of films were released each year in the seventies, and the forgettable ones stopped being shown decades ago. You are comparing this year's whole output against fifty years of filtering, which is not a comparison anyone can win.
cards.move: Every decade was mostly rubbish. Only the good part gets carried forward.
cards.trap: Comparing everything made now against what survived fifty years.
cards.reference: Taleb, Fooled by Randomness, Texere, 2001

cards.question: A street has four restaurants that have each been open thirty years. "This is a great street for restaurants." What is missing?
cards.answer: You cannot see the dozen that opened and shut on the same street. A street where restaurants fail fast and a street where they thrive both end up showing you only the ones still trading.
cards.move: Ask what used to be in the empty unit.
cards.trap: Only the survivors are still standing there to be counted.
cards.reference: Denrell, Vicarious Learning, Undersampling of Failure, and the Myths of Management, Organization Science, 2003

cards.question: A study of letters written home from a war finds morale was high. What should you check first?
cards.answer: Letters survive when someone kept them, which usually means the writer came home. Letters from those who did not are far likelier to have been lost — so the archive is filtered by the outcome you might be trying to study.
cards.move: An archive is not a sample. It is what somebody chose to keep.
cards.trap: Treating an archive as a sample of what was written.
cards.reference: Taleb, Fooled by Randomness, Texere, 2001

cards.question: A city puts speed cameras at its worst accident blackspots. Accidents there fall the following year. What is the safest reading?
options: Some of the fall would have happened anyway
The cameras made drivers worse elsewhere
cards.answer: Blackspots are picked in their worst year, and an unusually bad year is usually followed by a less bad one whatever you do. Some of the improvement is real and some is the site returning to its normal rate — separating them needs comparison sites, not before-and-after.
cards.move: A blackspot picked in its worst year would have eased on its own.
cards.trap: A site is chosen because it had an unusually bad year.
cards.source: Regression to the mean in road safety
cards.reference: Hauer, Observational Before-After Studies in Road Safety, Pergamon, 1997

cards.question: A struggling shop gets a new manager and takes more the next quarter. What would make the case convincing?
options: Other shops that kept their manager
cards.answer: You need shops that were also having a bad quarter and did not change manager. Without them, the ordinary bounce from a bad quarter and the effect of the new manager are the same number and cannot be told apart.
cards.move: The comparison you need is the one that did nothing.
cards.trap: The manager arrived precisely because the quarter was bad.
cards.source: Regression to the mean in management
cards.reference: Barnett, van der Pols & Dobson, Regression to the mean: what it is and how to deal with it, International Journal of Epidemiology, 2005

cards.question: A doctor is convinced a treatment works and prescribes it mainly to patients who are only mildly ill. What happens to their view?
cards.answer: Mild cases mostly recover anyway, so the treatment appears to work every time. The belief is not surviving a test, it is choosing patients who cannot disconfirm it — and the more it is confirmed the more confident it gets.
cards.move: Ask which patients would have proved you wrong, and whether you gave it to them.
cards.trap: Getting the result you expect feels like evidence for the belief.
cards.reference: Nickerson, Confirmation Bias: A Ubiquitous Phenomenon in Many Guises, Review of General Psychology, 1998

cards.question: You want to know whether a diet is working, so you weigh yourself whenever you feel lighter. What have you measured?
cards.answer: Choosing when to measure by how you feel makes the readings a record of your mood rather than your weight. A fixed schedule you cannot move is the whole difference between data and self-portraiture.
cards.move: Decide when you will measure before you know what it will say.
cards.trap: The measurement is triggered by the thing being measured.
cards.reference: Nickerson, Confirmation Bias: A Ubiquitous Phenomenon in Many Guises, Review of General Psychology, 1998

cards.question: A menu opens with a €95 tasting menu almost nobody orders. Why is it there?
cards.answer: The expensive item sets the scale everything else is read against. Its job is not to sell; it is to make the middle of the menu feel like restraint. Remove it and the same €40 dish starts to feel expensive.
cards.move: The dish nobody orders is doing most of the work on the menu.
cards.trap: Assuming a price is there to be paid.
cards.reference: Tversky & Kahneman, Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases, Science, 1974

cards.question: A charity asks whether you would give €500, then asks what you would actually give. Why not just ask the second question?
options: The first number moves the second
cards.answer: The opening number becomes the reference the real answer is judged against, and people asked the big question first give more. It works even when the first figure is obviously beyond what anyone would give.
cards.move: Whoever speaks first has already moved your number.
cards.trap: Believing your own figure came from your own budget.
cards.reference: Tversky & Kahneman, Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases, Science, 1974

cards.question: A radio phone-in finds 78% of callers oppose a new law. What has it measured?
options: Who felt strongly enough to ring
cards.answer: Phoning in costs time and requires a reason, so the line collects people with a strong view — usually against something. Ten thousand callers chosen by their own motivation tell you less than a thousand chosen at random.
cards.move: Anyone who selected themselves is not a sample of anybody else.
cards.trap: A large number of responses feels like a large sample.
cards.reference: Squire, Why the 1936 Literary Digest Poll Failed, Public Opinion Quarterly, 1988

cards.question: A gym reports that members who use the pool visit more often. Should it build another pool?
options: Only if the pool is full
cards.answer: People who come often have more chances to use the pool, so heavy users show up in the pool statistics whatever the pool does. The question is whether members who did not swim start coming more once they do — which this cannot answer.
cards.move: Frequent users turn up in every feature's numbers.
cards.trap: Reading a habit of the keenest members as a cause.
cards.reference: Hernán, Hernández-Díaz & Robins, A structural approach to selection bias, Epidemiology, 2004

cards.question: An airline surveys passengers at the gate about punctuality. What is skewed?
options: The badly delayed have gone home
cards.answer: Passengers whose flights were cancelled or badly delayed are not standing at the gate to be asked. The survey systematically misses the experiences it most needs.
cards.move: Ask where the people you need are, not where the people are.
cards.trap: Surveying where the people are, rather than where the answer is.
cards.reference: Hernán, Hernández-Díaz & Robins, A structural approach to selection bias, Epidemiology, 2004

cards.question: Children who own more books score better at school. Should the state post books to families?
cards.answer: Books in a house come with parents who read, time, income and quiet — any of which could do the work. Posting books tests whether the books mattered, and when it has been tried the effect is far smaller than the correlation suggested.
cards.move: The object in the house is rarely the thing doing the work.
cards.trap: A visible thing standing in for everything invisible around it.
cards.reference: Evans, Kelley, Sikora & Treiman, Family scholarly culture and educational success: Books and schooling in 27 nations, Research in Social Stratification and Mobility, 2010

cards.question: Neighbourhoods with more trees have lower crime. What is the most likely reading?
options: Both follow from money spent there
cards.answer: Streets get planted where a council invests, and investment brings lighting, repairs and maintenance with it. Trees may help — some trials suggest greening does — but the raw correlation is mostly a map of where money went.
cards.move: When two good things appear together, look for the third that bought both.
cards.trap: Two things moving together, and only one of them is easy to see.
cards.reference: Branas et al., Citywide cluster randomized trial to restore blighted vacant land and its effects on violence, crime, and fear, PNAS, 2018

cards.question: People who take vitamins live longer. What kind of person takes vitamins?
options: Someone already doing several other healthy things
cards.answer: Vitamin takers exercise more, smoke less, and see doctors sooner. Trials that assign vitamins at random to people who were not already taking them mostly find nothing, which is what the correlation was hiding.
cards.move: The healthy-user effect turns almost any voluntary habit into a miracle.
cards.trap: The pill is easy to measure; the life around it is not.
cards.reference: Bjelakovic et al., Antioxidant supplements for prevention of mortality in healthy participants and patients with various diseases, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2012

cards.question: A researcher measures 30 outcomes in one trial and reports the two that reached significance. What is the problem?
options: Two in thirty is what chance produces
cards.answer: At the usual threshold, roughly one measurement in twenty comes out significant by chance alone. Thirty measurements should produce about one or two even if nothing is happening. Reporting only those two turns noise into a finding.
cards.move: Ask how many things were measured before you ask what was found.
cards.trap: Reading a threshold designed for one question as if it survived thirty.
cards.reference: Goldacre et al., COMPare: a prospective cohort study correcting and monitoring 58 misreported trials in real time, Trials, 2019

cards.question: A company tries 12 subject lines and one gets a much better open rate. What should it do next?
options: Run that one again on its own
cards.answer: The best of twelve is the best partly because it caught a good sample. Running it alone against the original is what separates a real effect from the luckiest draw — and often it comes back to the middle.
cards.move: The winner of a big search has to win again to count.
cards.trap: The winner of a wide search is partly a winner by luck.
cards.reference: Kohavi, Tang & Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments, Cambridge University Press, 2020

cards.question: After a shark attack is in the news, what happens to how risky people rate swimming?
cards.answer: Risk feels like whatever the mind can picture fastest, and a vivid recent story is very fast. The measured jump is real and fades slowly, which is why coverage shapes fear far more than statistics do.
cards.move: Fear tracks vividness. It does not track frequency.
cards.trap: How easily an example comes to mind stands in for how often it happens.
cards.reference: Tversky & Kahneman, Availability: A heuristic for judging frequency and probability, Cognitive Psychology, 1973

cards.question: Which do people consistently overestimate: deaths from homicide, or from diabetes?
cards.answer: Homicide is reported and diabetes is not, so people overestimate the first and underestimate the second by large factors. What is dangerous and what is memorable are almost unrelated.
cards.move: The quiet causes are the big ones. That is why they are quiet.
cards.trap: Causes that make the news are the ones the mind reaches first.
cards.source: Lichtenstein et al., judged frequency of lethal events
cards.reference: Lichtenstein, Slovic, Fischhoff, Layman & Combs, Judged frequency of lethal events, Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory, 1978

cards.question: You are 200 pages into a 400-page novel you are not enjoying. What should decide whether you finish it?
cards.answer: The 200 read are gone whichever way you choose. The only live question is whether the next 200 beat anything else you could read — and the answer is usually no, which is why so many people finish books they disliked.
cards.move: The only pages that can still cost you are the ones ahead.
cards.trap: The pages behind you feel like an investment to protect.
cards.reference: Arkes & Blumer, The psychology of sunk cost, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 1985

cards.question: A team has spent nine months on a feature and new research says users do not want it. What is the right question?
options: How to salvage the nine months
Whether the next month is worth spending
cards.answer: The nine months are spent whatever happens next. Framing it as salvage is what turns a stopped project into a shipped one nobody uses, because it makes finishing feel like recovering rather than spending.
cards.move: You cannot get spent time back by spending more of it.
cards.trap: Nine months of work feels like something that can still be recovered.
cards.reference: Staw, Knee-deep in the big muddy: a study of escalating commitment to a chosen course of action, Organizational Behavior and Human Performance, 1976

cards.question: A test for a rare condition never gives a false negative but sometimes a false positive. You test negative. What do you know?
options: You almost certainly do not have it
cards.answer: A test that never misses makes a negative decisive: if you had it, the test would have said so. The same test's positives are weak, because false positives are the only kind of error it makes. One test, two very different kinds of answer.
cards.move: Ask which way the test can be wrong. It changes what each result means.
cards.trap: Treating positive and negative results as equally informative.
cards.reference: Eddy, Probabilistic reasoning in clinical medicine, in Kahneman, Slovic & Tversky (eds), Judgment under Uncertainty, Cambridge University Press, 1982

cards.question: Nine in ten people who take up rowing were swimmers. Does that mean swimming leads to rowing?
options: Not without knowing how many swimmers there are
cards.answer: That most rowers swam says nothing about how many swimmers row. If swimming is very common, almost every activity will be full of former swimmers without swimming leading anywhere in particular.
cards.move: "Most A are B" and "most B are A" are different sentences with different answers.
cards.trap: Reading the share one way round as if it read the other.
cards.reference: Eddy, Probabilistic reasoning in clinical medicine, in Kahneman, Slovic & Tversky (eds), Judgment under Uncertainty, Cambridge University Press, 1982

cards.question: Two engineers check the same drawing independently and both approve it. Is the drawing twice as safe?
options: Only if their mistakes are unrelated
cards.answer: Two checks only multiply if they can fail for different reasons. Trained the same way, working from the same brief, they tend to miss the same things — which is why serious systems try to make their checks disagree.
cards.move: Two checks that would fail together are one check.
cards.trap: Adding checks feels like multiplying safety.
cards.reference: Reason, Human Error, Cambridge University Press, 1990

cards.question: A portfolio holds thirty different technology companies. How diversified is it?
cards.answer: Diversification comes from holdings that fall for different reasons. Thirty companies exposed to the same rates, the same customers and the same supply chain behave in a crisis like a smaller number of positions.
cards.move: Count the reasons things could fall, not the number of things.
cards.trap: Counting holdings rather than the things that could sink them.
cards.reference: Markowitz, Portfolio Selection, Journal of Finance, 1952

cards.question: In a country of 60 million, roughly how often will a genuinely one-in-a-million event happen today?
cards.answer: Sixty million people each having a one-in-a-million day produces about sixty such days, today, and again tomorrow. Extraordinary coincidences are not evidence of anything: at scale they are compulsory.
cards.move: At a country's scale, the impossible happens daily and gets reported.
cards.trap: One in a million sounds like a synonym for never.
cards.source: The law of truly large numbers
cards.reference: Diaconis & Mosteller, Methods for Studying Coincidences, Journal of the American Statistical Association, 1989

cards.question: Someone dreams of an old friend and gets a call from them the next day. How surprising is it?
options: Not, given how many dreams and how many people
cards.answer: You have thousands of dreams a year about hundreds of people, and remember only the ones followed by something. The near-misses leave no trace, so the rate of coincidence is measured only from its successes.
cards.move: The hits get remembered and the misses never happened as far as you know.
cards.trap: Counting the hit and not the misses.
cards.reference: Diaconis & Mosteller, Methods for Studying Coincidences, Journal of the American Statistical Association, 1989

cards.question: A rumour reaches three new people a day, each of whom does the same. Roughly how long to reach a town of 20,000?
cards.answer: Three to the ninth is about 20,000. The first days look like nothing at all, which is exactly why anything spreading this way is always noticed too late to be stopped early.
cards.move: Nine days from one person to a whole town, and the first six look like nothing.
cards.trap: Repeated multiplication feels like repeated addition.
cards.reference: Bartlett, Forgotten Fundamentals of the Energy Crisis, American Journal of Physics, 1978

cards.question: A cost grows 3% a year and a budget grows 1%. After 30 years, how much larger is the cost relative to the budget?
cards.answer: The ratio grows at about 2% a year, and 1.02 to the thirtieth is roughly 1.8. Two points a year is not a small difference in the end; it is nearly double.
cards.move: Two percentage points, compounded for a career, is a doubling.
cards.trap: Reading a two-point gap as a small permanent difference.
cards.reference: Bartlett, Forgotten Fundamentals of the Energy Crisis, American Journal of Physics, 1978

cards.question: A hospital has a worse survival rate than the next one, but does better on both mild and severe cases. Which is better?
options: The one doing better on both
cards.answer: The first hospital takes more severe cases, and severe cases die more wherever they go. Comparing overall rates compares the patients, not the care — which is why crude league tables punish the hospitals that take the hardest work.
cards.move: A crude league table measures who walked in, not what was done.
cards.trap: The overall figure feels like the summary of the parts.
cards.reference: Julious & Mullee, Confounding and Simpson's paradox, BMJ, 1994

cards.question: A university's overall acceptance rate is lower for one group, yet higher in every single department. Possible?
options: Yes, if they apply to different departments
cards.answer: If one group applies mainly to departments that reject nearly everyone, its overall rate can be lower while it does better in each. The total and the parts are answering different questions.
cards.move: Before comparing totals, ask whether the two groups were doing the same thing.
cards.trap: Assuming the whole has to move with all of its parts.
cards.reference: Bickel, Hammel & O'Connell, Sex Bias in Graduate Admissions: Data from Berkeley, Science, 1975

cards.question: A firm's training course is followed by higher sales among those who took it. What is the missing number?
options: How the people who did not take it did
cards.answer: People who volunteer for training are already the ones putting effort in. Without the salespeople who did not take it — ideally chosen at random — the course and the kind of person who signs up cannot be separated.
cards.move: Every claim about an effect is a claim about what would have happened otherwise.
cards.trap: A before-and-after with no one to compare against.
cards.reference: Holland, Statistics and Causal Inference, Journal of the American Statistical Association, 1986

cards.question: A government says a scheme created 40,000 jobs. What has to be true for that to be the effect?
options: That those jobs would not otherwise exist
cards.answer: Some of those jobs would have been created anyway, and some were moved from elsewhere. The effect is the difference against a world without the scheme, which is harder to measure and much smaller than the headline.
cards.move: Ask what the number would have been anyway. That is the whole claim.
cards.trap: Counting what happened as if nothing else would have.
cards.reference: HM Treasury, The Green Book: Central Government Guidance on Appraisal and Evaluation, 2022

cards.question: Which is more likely next year: a serious flood in one named city, or a serious flood somewhere caused by a river breaching a defence?
options: The second, by a wide margin
cards.answer: The second covers every river and every defence, and the first is one city. Adding detail makes a forecast more believable and less likely at the same time — which is why detailed predictions win arguments and lose money.
cards.move: The more specific a forecast, the more convincing and the less likely.
cards.trap: A story with a mechanism in it feels more probable than a bare claim.
cards.reference: Tversky & Kahneman, Extensional versus intuitive reasoning: the conjunction fallacy in probability judgment, Psychological Review, 1983

cards.question: A shop sells 40% of its stock in a sale, then 40% of what is left the next week. What share is gone?
cards.answer: The second 40% is of the remaining 60%, so it clears 24%. Forty plus twenty-four is sixty-four per cent gone, and thirty-six left. Percentages of percentages never add.
cards.move: Two forty-per-cent cuts leave more than a fifth standing.
cards.trap: Adding two percentages that are taken of different things.
cards.reference: Paulos, Innumeracy: Mathematical Illiteracy and Its Consequences, Hill and Wang, 1988

cards.question: A queue moves at 6 people a minute and 200 people are ahead. How long to the front?
cards.answer: Two hundred divided by six is about 33. The useful habit is not the arithmetic but taking the rate and the amount separately: almost every waiting-time question is one division nobody performs.
cards.move: Two numbers and one division answers most waiting questions.
cards.trap: Estimating from how the queue feels rather than the rate.
cards.reference: Little, A Proof for the Queuing Formula: L = λW, Operations Research, 1961

cards.question: How much concrete has been poured?
cards.answer: Most of it recently. China used more cement in three years — roughly 2011 to 2013 — than the United States used across the entire twentieth century. The built world is not an inheritance from the distant past so much as something assembled within living memory.
cards.move: China poured more cement in three years than America did in a hundred.
cards.source: US Geological Survey; International Cement Review

cards.question: Where does new mercury pollution come from?
cards.answer: Mostly from people panning for gold. Small-scale artisanal mining, not heavy industry, is the largest single source of mercury released by humans — miners mix it with ore to bind the gold, then burn it off, usually with no protection and often near where they live.
cards.move: The biggest mercury polluter on Earth is people looking for gold by hand.
cards.reference: UNEP, Global Mercury Assessment 2018, 2019

cards.question: What is most vanilla made of?
cards.answer: Not vanilla. The overwhelming majority of vanillin is synthesised from petrochemicals or wood pulp. Real vanilla is so valuable per kilogram that Madagascan growers guard their vines, harvest early to prevent theft, and sometimes lose the crop to violence.
cards.move: Almost all the vanilla you have eaten came from wood pulp or oil.

cards.question: What runs out before oil?
cards.answer: Possibly phosphorus. There is no substitute for it in fertiliser and no way to synthesise it; economically minable phosphate rock sits in a handful of countries, with a very large share in one disputed territory. Meanwhile a great deal of it is flushed into the sea through sewage.
cards.move: You can invent a new energy source. You cannot invent a new element.
cards.source: USGS phosphate rock; Cordell et al., Global Environmental Change, 2009
